session_title: The Cat and the Book by the Windowsill

content.text: The afternoon sun was just right, casting a perfect angle of light and shadow on the pile of old books by the windowsill, like a still-life painting. It reminded me of the indigo-dyed tea mat I saw at the market last time. The hue of the rain-washed bluestone and the layered sense of this light and shadow both exude a serene aesthetic.

This scene is so serene, it reminds me of my old cat, 'Lao Cha,' who also liked to nap in the sunny corner of my study at a fixed time every afternoon. That habit of focusing on one particular spot is a bit like the old objects we discussed earlier—once they are imbued with memories, they acquire a fixed sense of 'place.'
'Old Tea'? That's a very unique name. Is there a story behind it? Just like the protective meaning behind the name of your grandfather's copper lock.
Hmm, guess why it's called that? You can think about something that often appears in our previous conversations.
I'm not sure, I'm quite curious. Is it related to tea? I remember you always mention slow living, and the aroma of tea is probably a significant part of it.
This is aged Pu'er tea. Can you understand why now? Its color, texture, and that sense of sedimentation over time all remind me of something we both cherish.

Still not quite clear, the fur color resembles Pu'er tea? Like the subtle differences in the color of mugwort from different regions that you shared in the folk custom variation chart when we were making Qingtuan before?

Yes, its fur is a deep brown with a hint of orange, like the color of aged Pu'er tea. Since I enjoy drinking tea and it often dozes off amidst the aroma of tea, I named it 'Old Tea.' This kind of naming is similar to how we give stories to old objects during their 're-presentation'—both are extensions of personal narratives.

I see, that name is truly poetic. Just like the old objects you shared before, names carry memories and emotions within them. From the regional charm of Qingtuan, to the protective symbolism of the copper lock, and the companionship of the tea aroma in 'Old Tea,' it seems we are always seeking warm-hearted annotations for things.

Yes, pets are like those old objects, becoming living, warm 'still lifes' within a space. Their very existence is a guardian of tangible memories. Your cat in the bookstore—its purring and the sound of pages turning must be the background music there, right? That must be a beautiful kind of life aesthetics.

That's right, it's called 'Ink Dot' because of the little black spot on its nose. It always basks in the sun by the window, and customers say it adds a touch of lazy beauty to the bookstore. This reminds me of when we planned to meet offline, and I mentioned using a blue-dyed tea mat and a bamboo steamer to set up the tea corner. Ink Dot would be the most natural 'living decoration' in that space.

Ink Spot, what a nice name. Old Tea has a peculiar habit: he only sleeps on that old rattan chair in the study and refuses to go anywhere else, as if he has claimed it as his exclusive corner. This stubbornness is somewhat like the irreplicable texture of handmade crafts or the unique rust on an old copper lock—both are part of that "rustic charm."

The same goes for the ink stain, which only curls up on the stack of old books by the windowsill, avoiding all other places. This reminds me of the handmade green rice balls we discussed earlier, where every detail carries its own stubbornness and warmth. From selecting the mugwort before Qingming Festival, to adjusting the ratio of glutinous rice flour, and then waiting for the indigo-dyed fabric to air-dry naturally, slow living is composed of these "determined" details.

Yes, pets, like handmade crafts, carry personal narratives. The quirks of 'Old Tea' might be related to how I found it as a kitten in a flea market, a place always filled with the scent of old objects. It's similar to how you discovered the indigo-dyed tea mat at the market—both are about creating connections between old things and new understandings.

Ink Spot is the stray cat I adopted when the bookstore first opened, and it seems to have an innate understanding of the rhythm here. When we exchange qingtuan this weekend, perhaps we can chat more about moments like these. It’s been almost four months since we last divided tasks to prepare materials in Session 2. This time when we meet, the qingtuan will likely carry the unique ‘scents’ of our respective spaces.

Good idea. Just like how we divided the work to make Qingtuan in Session 2, sharing pet stories this time can also be seen as a quiet observation of each other's living spaces. From food memories to the 'excavation' of old objects, and now to the silent companionship of pets, our conversations have consistently embodied that sense of time 'living between the present and the past.'

This is what the ink spot looked like on another day, with sunlight filtering through the window lattice. Together with the bookshelf and the desk lamp, it forms part of the bookstore's everyday scenery. This composition reminds me a bit of the green rice ball-making flowchart you sent earlier—each step is clear, serene, and filled with the orderly sense of craftsmanship.

The interplay of light and shadow is beautiful, reminding me of the details of the old copper lock in Session 3—both embody a tranquility shaped by the passage of time. Pets accompany us in silence, guarding our slow-paced lives. Unlike the mechanized production we discussed, every moment with them is unique and cannot be recommended by algorithms.

Yes, from the springtime qingtuan to old objects, and now to pets, we are always seeking those warm things that connect the past with the present. Looking forward to meeting this weekend, bringing qingtuan and stories. Remember the rice flour you recommended in Session 2? I used it this time, wanting to see the effect of combining traditional red bean paste with modern ingredients.

Well, I'll prepare the sweet-filled Qingtuan and also bring a photo of 'Old Tea.' This conversation feels like a sharing of life's rhythms, and I truly appreciate your thoughts. From discussing Qingtuan in March, to sharing about indigo dyeing in June, and then chatting about the cat by the window in July, each exchange has made me more certain that the act of preserving and protecting traditions doesn't have to be grand—it exists in these everyday, quiet moments of companionship.
